q: For a heading change of less than 30 degrees, what bank angle is used?
answer: A bank angle that equals the heading change
source: For turns of less than 30 degrees of heading change, use a bank angle that equals that change.

q: A heading change from 020 to 045 degrees is required. What bank angle?
source: For example, if a heading change from 020 degrees to 045 degrees were required (a 25-degree change), you would use a bank angle of 25 degrees.

q: If the heading change is 30 degrees or greater, what bank angle is used?
source: If the heading change is 30 degrees or greater, use a bank angle of 30 degrees.

q: Prior to entering a normal turn you should be:
answer: In straight-and-level flight with trim properly set
distractors: Slightly nose low with power reduced
At MRT with speed brakes in
In a slight climb with nose-up trim
source: Prior to entering the turn, you should be in straight-and-level flight with trim properly set.

q: As you roll into the turn you lose some vertical component of lift, so you must:
answer: Add power and aft stick (trim) to compensate
distractors: Reduce power and lower the nose
Add forward stick and reduce power
source: As you roll into the turn, you will lose some of the vertical component of lift, so you'll have to add power and aft stick (trim) to compensate.

q: What lead point is used for initiating the roll-out?
answer: Approximately 10% of the angle of bank
source: Use a lead point of approximately 10% of the angle of bank for initiating your roll-out.

q: As you roll out of the turn the aircraft has a tendency to:
answer: Climb, because the vertical component of lift increases
source: As you roll out of the turn, the vertical component of lift will increase and the aircraft will have a tendency to climb.

q: To counteract the climb tendency on roll-out you:
answer: Lower the nose to level flight reference and reduce power to the pre-turn setting
distractors: Raise the nose and add power
Hold the turn trim and reduce power to idle
source: To counteract this, lower the nose attitude back to level flight reference and reduce power to the pre-turn setting.

q: Any aft stick or trim added during the turn must:
answer: Come out when the turn is complete
distractors: Be held for the next turn
Be left in for level flight
source: Any aft stick or trim added during the turn will have to come out when the turn is complete.

q: Normal turns summary — Throttle:
answer: Increase as needed to maintain airspeed
distractors: Reduce as needed to maintain altitude
source: Throttle: Increase as needed to maintain airspeed

q: Normal turns summary — Pitch:
answer: As required to maintain level flight
source: Pitch: As required to maintain level flight

q: Normal turns summary — Lead point for roll-out:
source: Lead point for roll-out: 10% AOB

q: The turn pattern consists of:
answer: Three pairs of left and right turns
distractors: Two pairs of left and right turns
Three turns in the same direction
source: Consisting of three pairs of left and right turns, the turn pattern gives you practice in smoothly performing a series of linked turns at a constant altitude and airspeed.

q: Turn pattern, first set: 30-degree AOB turns for how much heading change each?
source: The turn consists of two 30-degree angle of bank turns for 60 degrees of heading change each, two 45-degree AOB turns for 90 degrees of heading change each, and two 60-degree AOB turns for 120 degrees of heading change each.

q: Turn pattern, second set: 45-degree AOB turns for how much heading change each?
source: The turn consists of two 30-degree angle of bank turns for 60 degrees of heading change each, two 45-degree AOB turns for 90 degrees of heading change each, and two 60-degree AOB turns for 120 degrees of heading change each.

q: Turn pattern, third set: 60-degree AOB turns for how much heading change each?
source: The turn consists of two 30-degree angle of bank turns for 60 degrees of heading change each, two 45-degree AOB turns for 90 degrees of heading change each, and two 60-degree AOB turns for 120 degrees of heading change each.

q: Which correctly lists the turn pattern sets (AOB / heading change)?
source: The turn consists of two 30-degree angle of bank turns for 60 degrees of heading change each, two 45-degree AOB turns for 90 degrees of heading change each, and two 60-degree AOB turns for 120 degrees of heading change each.

q: How do you set 45 degrees of bank on the ADI?
answer: Place the bank angle pointer halfway between the 30- and 60-degree scale markers
distractors: Place the pointer one third of the way past 30
Use the HUD pitch ladder only
source: Since there are no 45-degree bank angle scale markers on the ADI display, you must place the bank angle pointer halfway between the 30-degree and 60-degree bank angle scale markers.

q: Turn reversals in the turn pattern are executed:
distractors: After a full stop on original heading for 1 minute
source: Execute the turn reversals smoothly, with no straight-and-level legs.

q: At the end of the turn pattern you:
answer: Recover wings level on original heading
source: At the end of the maneuver, recover wings level on original heading.

q: Airspeed maintained throughout the turn pattern:
source: Throughout the maneuver, maintain altitude and 250 KIAS, adding more aft stick and more power for each set of turns.

q: For each successive set of turns in the turn pattern you add:
answer: More aft stick and more power
distractors: Less power and more aft stick
source: Throughout the maneuver, maintain altitude and 250 KIAS, adding more aft stick and more power for each set of turns.

q: When reversing turns, to avoid gaining altitude you:
answer: Ease the back stick as you apply reverse aileron
distractors: Add power as you apply reverse aileron
Pull more back stick through the reversal
source: When reversing turns, ease the back stick as you apply reverse aileron in order to avoid gaining altitude.

q: A 1/2 standard-rate turn is performed at what rate?
source: A 1/2 standard-rate turn (1/2 SRT) is performed at 1-1/2 degrees per second.

q: At 1/2 SRT, a 30-degree heading change takes:
source: Therefore, a heading change of 30 degrees will take 20 seconds to complete.

q: To achieve the 1/2 SRT rate at different airspeeds you must:
source: To accomplish this rate at different airspeeds, you will have to vary the bank angle.

q: Rule of thumb for 1/2 SRT bank angle between 15,000 and 20,000 ft:
source: A good rule of thumb for determining bank angle between 15,000 and 20,000 ft is to use approximately 10 percent of indicated airspeed.

q: The 10%-of-KIAS rule of thumb applies between which altitudes?
source: A good rule of thumb for determining bank angle between 15,000 and 20,000 ft is to use approximately 10 percent of indicated airspeed.

q: At higher altitudes, a 1/2 SRT requires:
answer: More bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed
distractors: Less bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed
source: At higher altitudes, you will need more bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed, while at lower altitudes you will need less bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed to maintain a 1/2 SRT.

q: At lower altitudes, a 1/2 SRT requires:
answer: Less bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed
distractors: More bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed
source: At higher altitudes, you will need more bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed, while at lower altitudes you will need less bank than 10 percent of indicated airspeed to maintain a 1/2 SRT.

q: At 250 KIAS and 18,000 ft, 1/2 SRT bank angle is approximately:
source: For example, at 250 KIAS and 18,000 ft, the bank angle would be approximately 25 degrees.

q: To establish and maintain a 1/2 SRT at any altitude, adjust bank to achieve:
answer: One needle-width of deflection on the turn needle
source: Establishing and maintaining a 1/2 standard-rate turn at any altitude requires that you monitor the turn needle and adjust the bank angle as necessary to achieve one needle-width of deflection.

q: The power setting for increasing airspeed depends on:
answer: The magnitude of the desired change
source: The power setting you use for increasing airspeed depends on the magnitude of the desired change.

q: For an airspeed increase of less than 20 kts, you:
answer: Advance the throttle beyond the setting for the new airspeed, then reduce to the approximate setting to maintain it
distractors: Advance to MRT, then reduce at a 5-kt lead
Advance exactly to the new-airspeed setting and wait
source: For an airspeed increase of less than 20 kts, you should advance the throttle beyond the power setting for the new airspeed, allowing the airspeed to increase, and then reduce the power to the approximate setting to maintain the new airspeed.

q: For airspeed increases greater than 20 kts, advance the power to:
distractors: Just beyond the setting for the new airspeed
source: For airspeed increases greater than 20 kts, advance the power to MRT.

q: Speed increase greater than 20 kts: at what lead do you reduce the throttle?
source: Then, at a lead of 5 kts from the desired airspeed, reduce the throttle setting to approximately that required for the new speed.

q: The MRT / 5-kt lead method is used when practicing which T-45C speed change?
source: Use this method when you practice the speed change from 200 to 250 KIAS in the T-45C.

q: For a normal airspeed decrease you:
answer: Reduce power below the requirement for the desired airspeed, then at a 5-kt lead advance power as required
distractors: Reduce to idle and extend speed brakes always
Reduce power exactly to the new setting
Raise the nose without changing power
source: To perform normal airspeed decreases, reduce the power below the power requirement for the desired airspeed, allowing the airspeed to decrease, and then at a lead point of 5 kts, advance power as required for the new airspeed.

q: Lead point for advancing power in a normal airspeed decrease:
source: ...and then at a lead point of 5 kts, advance power as required for the new airspeed.

q: As airspeed decreases, to maintain level flight you need:
source: As airspeed decreases, more nose up trim will be required to maintain level flight.

q: For large or rapid airspeed decreases you:
answer: Reduce the throttle to idle and fully extend the speed brakes
distractors: Reduce to 700 pph and lower the nose
Reduce throttle slightly and raise the nose
source: When making large or rapid airspeed decreases, reduce the throttle to idle and fully extend the speed brakes.

q: When you extend the speed brakes, expect:
answer: A pitch up, and retrim to maintain altitude
source: When you extend the speed brakes, expect a pitch up and anticipate the need to retrim the aircraft to maintain altitude.

q: In a rapid speed decrease, at what lead do you retract speed brakes and reset power?
source: Because the airspeed will rapidly decrease, you will need to use a 5-kt lead point to retract the speed brakes and reset the power to avoid undershooting your desired airspeed.

q: When you retract the speed brakes, anticipate:
source: Anticipate a pitch down when you retract the speed brakes.

q: The idle / full speed brake method is used when practicing which T-45C speed change?
source: Use this method when you practice the speed change from 250 to 200 KIAS in the T-45C.

source: Published "Lead Radials" (LR's) provide 2.0 nm lead to assist in turning to an intermediate or final approach course.

q: The decelerating level speed change in a 1/2 SRT practiced in BI advances the aircraft approximately:
source: The decelerating level speed change in a 1/2 standard rate turn practiced in BI will advance the aircraft approximately 2 NM.

q: If turns are flown at 250 KIAS, lead required is:
source: Slightly more lead will be required if turns are flown at 250 KIAS.

q: TACAN — slow to 200 KIAS at:
source: At 5-7 nm prior to the FAF, slow to 200 KIAS.

q: TACAN — configure for landing and perform the landing checklist at:
answer: 3-5 nm prior to FAF (speed brakes retracted)
source: Configure the aircraft for landing 3-5 nm prior to FAF and perform landing checklist (Speed brakes retracted).

q: TACAN — to the FAF you maintain:
source: Maintain published course and altitude to the FAF.

q: Lead all level offs by:
source: Lead all level offs by 10% of your VSI.

q: Low altitude TACAN/VOR DME approach procedures are:
answer: Essentially the same as those used for a high altitude penetration
distractors: Flown with no speed brakes ever
source: When executing a low altitude TACAN/VOR DME approach, the procedures are essentially the same as those used for a high altitude penetration.

q: TERPS speed criteria used when designing low altitude approaches:
source: When designing low altitude approaches, a 200 knot Terminal Instrument Procedures (TERPS) speed criteria is used.

q: Approaches involving a procedure turn should be flown at a maximum of:
source: As discussed earlier, approaches involving a procedure turn should be flown at a maximum airspeed of 200 KIAS.

q: A long No PT track or arc:
answer: May be flown at a higher airspeed if traffic permits
distractors: Must be flown at exactly 200 KIAS
source: A long No PT track or arc may be flown at a higher airspeed if traffic permits.

q: At the higher speed on a No PT track or arc, consider:
source: Consideration should be given to the larger turn radius required at the higher speed.

q: Speed brakes may be unnecessary prior to the FAF if:
answer: Slowing from 250 KIAS is not required prior to transitioning to the landing configuration
distractors: The approach has a procedure turn
source: Speed brakes may be unnecessary prior to the FAF if slowing from 250 KIAS is not required prior to transitioning to the landing configuration.

q: At the FAF (TACAN) you:
answer: Start the clock, extend speed brakes, report landing checklist complete on the ICS, make gear down call to ATC
distractors: Configure for landing and slow to 200 KIAS
Report leaving altitude and retract speed brakes
Report Platform and reset the LAW
source: At the FAF, start the clock, extend speed brakes, report landing checklist complete on the ICS and make gear down call to ATC.

q: At the FAF, the landing checklist complete report is made on ___ and the gear down call to ___.
source: At the FAF, start the clock, extend speed brakes, report landing checklist complete on the ICS and make gear down call to ATC.

q: Speed brake extension at the FAF requires:
answer: Forward stick pressure to counter the pitch up
distractors: Aft stick to counter the pitch down
source: Forward stick pressure will be required to counter the pitch up due to speed brake extension.

q: After the FAF, descend to the MDA while monitoring ___ for the MAP.
source: Descend to the MDA and start looking for the runway while monitoring your DME for the MAP.

q: Plan your descent to be in level flight at the MDA:
source: Plan your descent to be in level flight at the MDA prior to reaching the MAP.

q: Maximum descent rate from the FAF (TACAN):
source: Do not exceed 1,000 fpm.

q: Keep heading changes small so you don't chase:
answer: The final approach course on the HSI or the course situation steering arrow on the HUD
source: Keep heading changes small so you don't chase the final approach course on the HSI display or the course situation steering arrow on the HUD.

q: Approximately 100 feet prior to the MDA you:
answer: Add about 300 pph fuel flow and apply slight backstick pressure
distractors: Reduce about 300 pph and push forward
source: Approximately 100 feet prior to the MDA, add about 300 pph fuel flow and apply slight backstick pressure to level off at MDA.

q: How much fuel flow is added to level off at MDA?
source: Approximately 100 feet prior to the MDA, add about 300 pph fuel flow and apply slight backstick pressure to level off at MDA.

q: At the MAP without the runway environment in sight or unable to land safely:
source: When you reach the MAP, if you don't have the runway environment in sight or determine that a safe landing is not possible, execute a missed approach.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: The two basic types of ground-controlled approaches are:
source: There are two basic types of ground-controlled approaches—the precision radar approach (PAR) and the surveillance radar approach (ASR).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: A PAR provides:
answer: Precise course, glidepath, and range information (precision approach)
distractors: Course, range and recommended altitudes only
source: A PAR provides you with precise course, glidepath, and range information and is classified as a precision approach.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: An ASR provides:
answer: Lower resolution course and range information only (no glideslope); non-precision
source: An ASR (commonly referred to as a surveillance approach) provides lower resolution course and range information only (no glideslope) and is classified as a non-precision approach.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Glideslope is defined as:
answer: The descent angle assigned to an approach to a given runway for obstacle clearance and/or signal reception
distractors: The portion of a precision approach that intercepts the azimuth of an ILS or the FAC of a PAR
The 300 ft per mile recommended altitudes
source: Glideslope is defined as the descent angle assigned to an approach to a given runway for obstacle clearance and/or signal reception.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Glidepath is defined as:
answer: The portion of a precision approach that intercepts the azimuth of an ILS approach or the FAC of a PAR approach
distractors: The descent angle assigned for obstacle clearance
source: Glidepath is defined as the portion of a precision approach that intercepts the azimuth of an ILS approach or the FAC of a PAR approach.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: PAR and ASR approaches are divided into which two segments?
source: Both the PAR and ASR approaches are divided into two segments, initial pattern and final approach.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: During the initial pattern of an ASR or PAR you are guided by:
source: During the initial pattern of an ASR or PAR approach, you will be guided by surveillance radar.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: The initial pattern segment ends when the aircraft is inbound on the FAC at approximately:
source: This segment includes all maneuvering up to the point at which your aircraft is inbound on the final approach course and at approximately 8 nm from touchdown.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: During the transition to final, the GCA controller directs:
source: During the transition to final, the GCA controller will direct your headings and altitudes.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Controller instructions to initiate turns and descents should be complied with:
source: All controller instructions to initiate turns and descents should be complied with immediately.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: In the GCA pattern, turns are:
answer: Standard rate, not to exceed 30 degrees AOB
distractors: Half standard rate, not to exceed 10 degrees
source: In the pattern, maintain standard rate turns not to exceed 30 degrees AOB.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: On final, AOB should approximate the degrees to be turned, not to exceed:
source: On final, your AOB should approximate the number of degrees to be turned not to exceed half standard rate (approximately 10 degrees AOB).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Good technique for AOB turning base to final:
source: A good technique is 30 degrees AOB in pattern, 20 degrees AOB turning base to final.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Good technique for AOB in the GCA pattern:
source: A good technique is 30 degrees AOB in pattern, 20 degrees AOB turning base to final.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Once on final, max AOB for heading corrections to course:
source: Once on final, do not exceed 10 degrees AOB for heading corrections to course.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Radar approach minimums can be found:
answer: In FLIP instrument approach procedure publications — on the approach plates and in the radar approach minimums section
source: Radar approach minimums can be found in the FLIP instrument approach procedure publications, both on the approach plates and in the radar approach minimums section (Figure 6-29).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Absolute minimums when single-piloted:
source: Although some published approach minimums are lower than 200-1/2, you are limited to absolute minimums of 200-1/2 when single-piloted.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: During a GCA, the controller continuously feeds you:
answer: Course and heading information, and on a PAR, glidepath information on final
distractors: Glidepath information on both PAR and ASR
source: During a GCA, your position in the pattern and on final will be directed by a controller who will continuously feed you course and heading information and, in the case of a PAR approach, glidepath information on final.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: In the GCA pattern you must acknowledge all radio calls and read back:
answer: All headings, altitudes, and altimeter settings
source: In the pattern, you are required to acknowledge all radio calls and read back all headings, altitudes, and altimeter settings.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Per FAR 7110.65 the controller is required to give:
answer: Missed approach instructions, weather (if less than VFR), altimeter, and lost comm instructions (if likely to encounter IMC)
source: According to FAR 7110.65, the controller is required to give missed approach instructions, weather conditions (if less than VFR), altimeter, and lost comm instructions (if likely to encounter IMC).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Per FAR 7110.65, weather conditions are given when:
source: ...weather conditions (if less than VFR)...

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Per FAR 7110.65, lost comm instructions are given when:
distractors: Only if less than VFR at the field
source: ...lost comm instructions (if likely to encounter IMC).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: In the pattern, the controller must communicate with you at least:
source: In the pattern, the controller must communicate with you at least once a minute and you are required to acknowledge the controller's calls.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: In the pattern, if you hear no transmissions for more than ___ seconds, attempt to contact the controller.
source: If you hear no transmissions for more than 60 seconds, attempt to contact the controller.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: In the pattern, if unable to reestablish contact you:
answer: Comply with the lost communication instructions
source: If you are unable to reestablish contact, then comply with the lost communication instructions.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Controller info furnished in the pattern — item 1:

Advisory to perform landing check (USN/USMC controllers only)
Missed approach and lost communication instructions

distractors: Location of the missed approach point (MAP) (surveillance only)
Advisory to perform landing check (USN/USMC controllers only)
Missed approach and lost communication instructions

Missed approach and lost communication instructions
source: 3. Location of the missed approach point (MAP) (surveillance only)

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Controller info furnished in the pattern — item 4:
answer: Advisory to perform landing check (USN/USMC controllers only)
distractors: Type of approach to expect (precision or surveillance)
Location of the missed approach point (MAP) (surveillance only)
source: 4. Advisory to perform landing check (USN/USMC controllers only)

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Controller info furnished in the pattern — item 5:
answer: Missed approach and lost communication instructions
distractors: Type of approach to expect (precision or surveillance)
Location of the missed approach point (MAP) (surveillance only)
source: 5. Missed approach and lost communication instructions

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Which is NOT on the list of information the controller furnishes in the pattern?
distractors: Missed approach and lost communication instructions
source: 1. Type of approach to expect (precision or surveillance) 2. Duty runway 3. Location of the missed approach point (MAP) (surveillance only) 4. Advisory to perform landing check (USN/USMC controllers only) 5. Missed approach and lost communication instructions

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: The location of the MAP is furnished in the pattern for:
source: 3. Location of the missed approach point (MAP) (surveillance only)

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: The advisory to perform landing check is given by:
source: 4. Advisory to perform landing check (USN/USMC controllers only)

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Besides the listed items, the controller also gives:
answer: Position information and heading changes as necessary to keep you on course
source: Additionally, the controller will give you position information and heading changes as necessary to keep you on course.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Final controller radio check as you commence final:
answer: "THIS IS MCCAIN FINAL CONTROLLER. HOW DO YOU HEAR?"
source: As you commence your final approach, the final controller will perform a radio check; "THIS IS MCCAIN FINAL CONTROLLER. HOW DO YOU HEAR?"

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Your response to the final controller's radio check:
answer: "LOUD AND CLEAR, THREE DOWN AND LOCKED" (or position of gear)
source: You should respond with "LOUD AND CLEAR, THREE DOWN AND LOCKED" (or position of gear).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: After the radio check, the controller may also tell you:
answer: That you need not acknowledge further transmissions
distractors: To read back every heading on final
source: The controller may also tell you that you need not acknowledge further transmissions.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: On final, the controller must contact you at least every ___ on a PAR.
source: On final approach, the controller is required to make contact with you at least every 5 seconds on a PAR or 15 seconds on an ASR.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: On final, the controller must contact you at least every ___ on an ASR.
source: On final approach, the controller is required to make contact with you at least every 5 seconds on a PAR or 15 seconds on an ASR.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Comm intervals — pattern / PAR final / ASR final:
source: In the pattern, the controller must communicate with you at least once a minute … at least every 5 seconds on a PAR or 15 seconds on an ASR.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: If you lose contact on final for the respective time for the approach being flown:
answer: Attempt to recontact; if not successful, execute the lost communication instructions
distractors: Execute the missed approach immediately without trying
source: If you lose contact with the controller for the respective amount of time for the approach being flown, attempt to recontact and if not successful, execute the lost communication instructions.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: GCA pattern entry configuration — Airspeed:
source: Airspeed: 200 KIAS

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: GCA pattern entry configuration — Gear:
source: Gear: Up

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: GCA pattern entry configuration — Speed brakes:
source: Speed brakes: In

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: GCA pattern entry configuration — Flaps/slats:
source: Flaps/slats: Up

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: GCA pattern entry configuration — Available NAVAIDS:
source: Available NAVAIDS: Tuned

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: The downwind leg is normally flown:
answer: Straight and level at 200 KIAS and pattern altitude
source: Normally, you fly the first leg of the pattern (the downwind leg) straight and level at 200 KIAS and pattern altitude.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: At the end of the downwind leg, the controller directs a turn to:
source: At the end of the downwind leg, the controller will direct a turn to base leg.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: At the end of the base leg, the controller directs a turn to:
answer: Either a dogleg or the final approach course
source: At the end of the base leg, the controller will direct a turn to either a dogleg or the final approach course.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: On base or a dogleg, unless directed by ATC, stay clean at 200 KIAS until within:
answer: 10 nm of the field and 30 radials of the FAC
source: Once established on base leg or on a dogleg to the FAC, unless directed by ATC, stay clean and at 200 KIAS until you are within 10 nm of the field and 30 radials of the final approach course.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: When within those parameters, you transition to landing configuration and slow to:
answer: 150 KIAS (speed brakes retracted, complete landing checklist)
source: When within those parameters, transition to landing configuration, speed brakes retracted, slow to 150 KIAS, and complete the landing checklist (speed brakes retracted).

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: After configuring in the GCA pattern you will have to:
answer: Retrim the nose to maintain level flight
source: You will have to retrim the nose to maintain level flight.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: Slow to on-speed when:
answer: Within 10 nm and on an intercept heading within 30 degrees of the FAC
source: When within 10 nm and on an intercept heading that is within 30 degrees of the final approach course, slow to on-speed.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: USN/USMC controllers' "PERFORM LANDING CHECKS" on the base leg is:
answer: Only a reminder; it does not direct the pilot to dirty up
distractors: A directive to slow to approach speed
source: USN/USMC controllers will state "PERFORM LANDING CHECKS" on the base leg; this is only a reminder and does not direct the pilot to dirty up.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: If the controller says "SLOW TO APPROACH SPEED":
answer: It is directed for sequencing; comply or state that you are unable
source: If the controller says, "SLOW TO APPROACH SPEED," the controller is directing this for sequencing and the aircrew must comply or state that they are unable.

topic: PAR Approach — GCA Basics, Comms & Pattern
q: GCAs can be flown in which flap configurations?
source: GCAs can be flown at full, one-half, and no-flap configurations.

q: At the beginning of a PAR final you are:
answer: Straight and level, on-speed, normally at approximately 1,500 ft AGL
source: At the beginning of a PAR final approach, you will be straight and level, on-speed, and normally at approximately 1,500 ft AGL.

q: Normal altitude at the beginning of a PAR final:
source: ...normally at approximately 1,500 ft AGL.

q: PAR final — restrict AOB to:
answer: Approximate degrees to be turned, not to exceed 1/2 SRT (approximately 10 degrees)
source: Restrict AOB to the approximate number of degrees to be turned, not to exceed 1/2 SRT (approximately 10 degrees).

q: PAR final — verify:
answer: Gear down, flaps at half or full
source: Verify gear down, flaps at half or full.

q: PAR final — trim the aircraft for:
source: Trim aircraft for hands off level flight.

q: On a PAR, when told "ON GLIDEPATH" you:
answer: Extend the speed brakes and adjust power as required to establish a descent
source: When the controller informs you that you are "ON GLIDEPATH," extend the speed brakes and adjust power as required to establish a descent.

q: Initially after speed brake extension on the PAR you need:
answer: Forward stick pressure to counter the pitch up
distractors: Aft stick to counter a pitch down
source: Forward stick pressure will initially be required to counter the pitch up caused by speed brake extension.

q: PAR ICS report after establishing the descent:
distractors: "LOUD AND CLEAR, THREE DOWN AND LOCKED"
source: Report, "SPEED BRAKES FULL, LANDING CHECKLIST COMPLETE," on the ICS.

q: PAR rate of descent varies with:
source: The rate of descent will vary for different glideslope angles and groundspeeds.

q: Where is the rate of descent chart for a given glideslope and groundspeed?
answer: Inside back cover of the approach plates
distractors: Front cover of the approach plates
source: The inside back cover of the approach plates contains a chart that will provide you rate of descent for a given glideslope and groundspeed.

q: On PAR final, adjust power to:
answer: Maintain your rate of descent and keep the aircraft on-speed
source: Adjust power to maintain your rate of descent and keep the aircraft on-speed.

q: PAR heading corrections — bank angle:
source: When making heading corrections, try to keep the amount of bank angle small (5-10 degrees) so that you don't end up chasing the heading.

q: On the PAR, if you get off heading:
answer: Don't try to correct to course; return to your last assigned heading with smooth inputs
source: If you get off heading, don't try to correct to course. Use smooth control inputs and return to your last assigned heading.

q: As you near the decision altitude, begin:
answer: An "inside/outside" scan to visually acquire the runway environment
source: As you near the decision altitude, begin an "inside/outside" scan to visually acquire the runway environment.

q: PAR — no runway environment in sight at the DA:
answer: Execute a missed approach (make the mandatory missed approach call)
distractors: Level off at DA and continue to MAP
source: If you do not have the runway environment in sight when you reach the DA, execute a missed approach (make the mandatory missed approach call).

q: On the ASR final, the controller cannot furnish:
source: On the ASR final approach, the controller cannot furnish glideslope information.

q: On an ASR, who establishes and maintains the correct rate of descent?
source: It will be up to you to establish and maintain the correct rate of descent.

q: ASR — the controller identifies the MAP:
answer: In nautical miles from the end of the runway
source: The controller will identify the missed approach point (MAP) in nautical miles from the end of the runway, and will direct the descent by stating, "BEGIN DESCENT."

q: ASR — the controller directs the descent by stating:
source: ...and will direct the descent by stating, "BEGIN DESCENT."

q: ASR recommended altitudes each mile are provided:
source: On pilot request, the controller will provide recommended altitudes each mile on final.

q: ASR recommended altitudes decrease:
source: Recommended altitudes decrease 300 ft per mile (approximates a 3-degree glideslope).

q: To smoothly level at MDA prior to the MAP, your altitudes should be:
source: In order to smoothly level at MDA prior to the MAP, your altitudes should be slightly lower than those recommended.

q: ASR descent rate (depending on groundspeed) to reach MDA prior to MAP:
source: Depending on your groundspeed, a descent rate of 800-1000 fpm will allow you to descend to the MDA prior to reaching the MAP.

q: ASR — approximately 100 ft prior to MDA:
answer: Add about 300 pph fuel flow and apply slight backstick pressure
distractors: Retract speed brakes and add MRT
source: Approximately 100 feet prior to MDA, add about 300 pph fuel flow and apply slight backstick pressure to level off at MDA.

q: ASR — upon reaching the MAP without the runway or unable to land safely:
answer: Execute the missed approach as instructed
source: Upon reaching the MAP, if you do not have the runway in sight or are otherwise unable to perform a safe landing, execute the missed approach as instructed.

q: Decision altitude (DA) is used on the ___; MDA/MAP on the ___.
source: If you do not have the runway environment in sight when you reach the DA, execute a missed approach … Upon reaching the MAP, if you do not have the runway in sight … execute the missed approach as instructed.
